name: Fear of missing out
statement: People who score higher on the fear-of-missing-out scale report using social media more, and report worse mood and lower life satisfaction.
meaning: Przybylski and colleagues define fear of missing out as a pervasive apprehension that others might be having rewarding experiences from which one is absent, marked by a desire to stay continually connected with what others are doing. It is framed as an individual difference, a trait some people carry more of, rather than a state a situation produces. Everything in the founding paper rests on one self-report instrument, the ten-item Fear of Missing Out scale, and every correlation below is between that scale and another questionnaire. Two of its ten items are about behaviour rather than fear: item 8 asks whether sharing details of a good time online is important, item 10 whether the respondent keeps tabs on friends while on holiday. That matters because the finding the construct is famous for is a correlation between this scale and self-reported social media use, and part of the scale is already asking about social media use.

origin.who: Andrew K. Przybylski, Kou Murayama, Cody R. DeHaan and Valerie Gladwell
origin.note: Three cross-sectional studies that built the scale and mapped its correlates. The term was already in circulation: the paper cites two 2011 and 2012 trend reports by the marketing agency JWT and columns in the New York Times and San Francisco Chronicle as the writing it drafted its items from.

evidence: Study 1 gave 32 candidate items to 1,013 Mechanical Turk workers, 672 men and 341 women, aged 18 to 62, of whom 41.1% lived in the United States and 35.9% in India. An iterative confirmatory factor analysis cut the pool to 25 items, and item response theory picked the final ten. Their combined test information peaked at a latent trait level of .51, and the ten items gave an alpha of .87. Study 2 ran the scale on a Harris Poll panel in Great Britain over two weeks in late September 2011, yielding 2,079 working-age adults, 1,040 men and 1,039 women aged 22 to 65. FoMO correlated −.37 with age, −.29 with psychological need satisfaction, −.24 with general mood, −.19 with life satisfaction and .40 with social media engagement. Engagement was measured by five questions about using social media around waking, meals and sleep. Mediation analysis found that need satisfaction, mood and life satisfaction predicted social media engagement only through FoMO, the direct paths falling to b = .003, b = .001 and b = .013, none of them significant. Study 3 tested 87 first-year students, 20 men and 67 women. FoMO predicted Facebook engagement at b = .41, negative affect while using Facebook at .40, positive affect at .31, Facebook use during lectures at .27, p = .013, and self-reported distracted driving at .28, p = .029. The driving figure rests on the 62 participants who were regular drivers rather than on all 87, and 64 of the 87 reported using Facebook in no lectures at all. All three studies were one-time surveys, and the authors say so, writing that future work in experimental settings would allow causal models to be evaluated.

replication.headline: The correlation with social media use reproduces at .38 to .41 across two large meta-analyses, close to the original .40, while the scale's structure and the causal reading of it do not hold up.
replication.detail: Akbari and colleagues reviewed 86 effect sizes covering 55,134 participants, mean age 22.07, 58.37% female. Their pooled internet-use estimate rests on 85 of those effect sizes: r = 0.41, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.44. That is close to the .40 Przybylski reported in one British panel. It is also heterogeneous enough that the average is a poor summary, with I-squared 94.04 and a 95% prediction interval running from 0.11 to 0.63. Trim and fill added 18 studies to the right of the mean and raised the estimate to r = 0.46, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.49, and the Egger test behind that is printed as one-tailed, t(84) = 2.190, p = 0.015. Facebook use gave r = 0.35, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.42, from 11 samples. Instagram use gave r = 0.49, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.64, from three, and its prediction interval runs from −0.97 to 0.99. The pandemic was the one moderator to reach significance, 58 pre-COVID samples at 0.38 against 14 later ones at 0.54, while the meta-regression model as a whole did not, F(15, 56) = 1.52, p = 0.130. Zhang, Li and Yu pooled 65 studies, 70 independent samples and 61,893 participants and got r = 0.38, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.41, with I-squared 94.65. The number depends on what is measured: addiction 0.47, intensity 0.32, duration 0.25 and frequency 0.14. That last estimate rests on five samples and does not clear the usual threshold, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.27, z = 1.95, two-tailed p = 0.051, and frequency of use is the most literal reading of 'uses social media more'. Zhang, Shang, Tian, Zhu and Zhang later pooled 85 studies and 90 effect sizes on mobile phone addiction and got r = 0.47, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.50, with I-squared 95.65. The structure of the scale is where the two large tests disagree. Groenestein and colleagues invited 10,226 members of a Dutch panel, and analysed the 2,041 respondents who used social media and passed a quality check. A two-dimension model fitted better than a single factor, CFI .954 against .912 and RMSEA .083 against .113, the dimensions being pervasive apprehension and desire for connection. Apprehension tracked problematic social media use more closely, r = .625 against .548, which is the reverse of what they predicted. Desire for connection tracked use frequency, .252 against .193, and extraversion, .130 against .010, and the frequency gap sits at p = .048. Elhai, Gazit, Casale and Montag collected 422 responses at a Midwestern American university and analysed 388. They found the opposite pattern on problematic smartphone use, connection desire r = 0.600 against apprehension 0.493, Wald chi-square(1) = 6.816, p = 0.009. Problematic social media use related equally to both, 0.600 against 0.552, p = 0.122, as did depression, anxiety, rumination and distress tolerance. Their two-factor model beat one factor, chi-square difference(1) = 11.430, p = 0.0007, and they note the gain was small, a CFI difference of 0.002. On direction, Li and colleagues followed 1,419 Dutch adolescents aged 11 to 15 across four annual waves from 2015 to 2019 with a random intercept cross-lagged panel model. Their abstract reports that within persons FoMO increased problematic social media use in mid-adolescence and not the reverse, and that low life satisfaction predicted rising FoMO in early adolescence. That is one study, in one country, on problematic use rather than use.

study.cite: Akbari, M., Seydavi, M., Palmieri, S., Mansueto, G., Caselli, G., & Spada, M. M. (2021). Fear of missing out (FoMO) and internet use: A comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Behavioral Addictions, 10(4), 879-900.

limits: Almost the whole literature is cross-sectional self-report, and the two things being correlated are measured minutes apart in the same questionnaire. Akbari and colleagues state the limit plainly: findings should be read in light of the observational nature of the review, and causality could not be inferred given the cross-sectional design of the included studies. Their samples were 45% Asian, 32% European, 19% American and 4% from Oceania, and young, so the pooled figure is not a general population figure. Recent pooling extends the correlation past use itself. Brombach, Kuhn, Eads and Dietch gathered 22 studies, 25 independent samples and 12,191 participants on FoMO and sleep. Sleep quality gave Fisher's Z = 0.265, 95% CI 0.101 to 0.429, across twelve samples with I-squared 98, and bedtime procrastination gave Z = 0.2305, 95% CI 0.0903 to 0.371, across four. Several figures could not be obtained. Fioravanti and colleagues pooled 33 independent samples and 21,473 participants, and their abstract at the University of Florence repository says the correlations with social networking site use and with problematic use were positive and robust without printing a number; ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403 on both attempts, so no effect size from it appears above. Li and colleagues' article is open access, and ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403 for it too, so its cross-lagged coefficients are described from the abstract at the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam repository and no coefficient from it is printed. Milyavskaya and colleagues' paper carries two studies, the second described in its abstract as experimental; Springer offers the full text at USD 39.95 and no figure from it is quoted here. Searches covered Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, PMC, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Springer, ScienceDirect, SSRN, the Vrije Universiteit and University of Florence repositories, Cyberpsychology, Acta Psychologica Sinica and general web search. They turned up longitudinal work and no experiment that manipulates social media exposure and measures fear of missing out.
misreadings: The prevalence claim is the loudest error. The figure that nearly three quarters of young adults experience FoMO comes from JWT trend reports of 2011 and 2012, which is where this entry reads it, in Przybylski's summary of them. It is marketing research, not a measured prevalence, and the founding paper calls it preliminary industry work. The second error is causal. A correlation of about .4 between two questionnaires filled in at the same sitting does not show that social media produces FoMO, or that FoMO drives people to social media, and the one four-wave study located here points the arrow from FoMO to problematic use rather than back. The third is treating FoMO research as part of the screen-time debate. Orben and Przybylski's specification curve analysis of three datasets, 355,358 adolescents, found digital technology use explained at most 0.4% of the variation in well-being, with a median standardised coefficient of −.035 in the American health survey. They report that regularly eating potatoes was nearly as negatively associated with well-being as technology use, and that wearing glasses was more so. That is a different measure of a different thing, and it is not a small-effect verdict on FoMO. The last is that the two-dimension finding is settled. Two large samples do split the scale in two, and they disagree about which dimension goes with problematic use, so a short form that drops items from one of them measures something other than what the original scale measured.
